youtube.title: Why Does Svalbard Have No Visa?
youtube.description:
Svalbard is Norwegian, yet a 1920 treaty gives citizens of more than 40 countries the right to live and work there, and Norway asks no nationality for a visa or work permit. Why did Norway accept an open door on its own land, and why does a Russian state company still run a mining town on the islands?

On the map, we follow the islands from a Dutch sighting in 1596 to the treaty of 1920, the fisheries zone of 1977 and the disputes over fish, seabed and satellites today. Norway's view and Russia's case are both given, and we look at three ways the map could change.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: Longyearbyen is about 1,310 km from the North Pole (said as 1,300 km in the opening)
sources.source: Great-circle distance from Longyearbyen (78.22°N) to 90°N; Norwegian Mapping Authority coordinates

sources.claim: Longyearbyen is about 960 km north of Tromsø
sources.source: Great-circle distance Tromsø (69.65°N, 18.96°E) to Longyearbyen (78.22°N, 15.63°E); Avinor route data

sources.claim: Svalbard lies between 74 and 81 degrees north
sources.source: Norwegian Polar Institute, 'About Svalbard'

sources.claim: The islands cover about 61,000 square kilometres
sources.source: Statistics Norway (SSB), land area of Svalbard 61,022 km²

sources.claim: Slightly more than the whole of Croatia
sources.source: Croatian Bureau of Statistics: land area 56,594 km²

sources.claim: More than half of the land lies under glaciers
sources.source: Norwegian Polar Institute: glaciers cover about 57% of Svalbard

sources.claim: About two thirds of the land is protected nature
sources.source: Norwegian Environment Agency / Governor of Svalbard: about 65% of land area protected

sources.claim: About 2,500 people live in the Norwegian settlements
sources.source: Statistics Norway, Population of Svalbard, 1 January 2024

sources.claim: Barentsburg lies about 36 km west-southwest of Longyearbyen in a straight line
sources.source: Great-circle distance between Norwegian Polar Institute place-name coordinates (TopoSvalbard): Longyearbyen 78.2232°N 15.6267°E, Barentsburg 78.0648°N 14.2335°E, about 36 km

sources.claim: Barentsburg is a Russian coal town of a few hundred people
sources.source: Statistics Norway, Population of Svalbard (Russian and Ukrainian settlements), 2024

sources.claim: Barentsburg's mine belongs to Arktikugol, a Russian state company
sources.source: Trust Arktikugol company information; Store norske leksikon, 'Arktikugol'

sources.claim: Pyramiden was closed in 1998
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Pyramiden'

sources.claim: About one resident in three in the Norwegian settlements is a foreign citizen; largest groups from Thailand, Sweden and the Philippines
sources.source: Statistics Norway, Population of Svalbard, 2024

sources.claim: About 50 nationalities live in Longyearbyen
sources.source: Longyearbyen Community Council (Longyearbyen lokalstyre)

sources.claim: Article 3 gives treaty nationals equal liberty of access and entry and equal rights to maritime, industrial, mining and commercial operations
sources.source: Treaty concerning the Archipelago of Spitsbergen, Paris, 9 February 1920, Articles 2 and 3

sources.claim: More than 40 countries are parties to the treaty, including China, India and the US
sources.source: Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs; French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs (treaty depositary), list of parties

sources.claim: No visa or work permit is needed for Svalbard, whatever the nationality; Svalbard is outside Schengen, and those who need a Schengen visa must have one to travel via mainland Norway
sources.source: Governor of Svalbard (Sysselmesteren), 'Entry and residence'

sources.claim: The Governor can refuse or remove people who cannot support themselves
sources.source: Regulations on rejection and expulsion of persons from Svalbard (Forskrift om bortvisning og utvisning fra Svalbard), 1995

sources.claim: Few care services; residents are expected to support themselves
sources.source: Governor of Svalbard, 'Moving to Svalbard'; Norwegian White Paper Meld. St. 32 (2015-2016) Svalbard

sources.claim: Governor's office urges carrying protection against polar bears outside settlements
sources.source: Governor of Svalbard, polar bear safety guidance

sources.claim: Willem Barentsz sighted the islands in June 1596 seeking a northern route to Asia, and named them Spitsbergen
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Willem Barentsz'; Norwegian Polar Institute history

sources.claim: The Dutch built the whaling station Smeerenburg in 1619
sources.source: Norwegian Polar Institute; Directorate for Cultural Heritage, Smeerenburg

sources.claim: England, the Netherlands and Denmark-Norway each claimed the islands during the whaling era
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbards historie'

sources.claim: John Munro Longyear founded the mining town in 1906
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Longyearbyen'; Arctic Coal Company records

sources.claim: British, Swedish, Russian and Norwegian companies staked claims before 1920
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbards historie'; Berg, R., 'From Spitsbergen to Svalbard', Polar Record, 2013

sources.claim: Norway, Sweden and Russia held conferences in Kristiania in 1910, 1912 and 1914, which failed
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbardtraktaten'; Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, history of the Svalbard Treaty

sources.claim: Nine signatory powers signed the treaty on 9 February 1920, giving Norway full and absolute sovereignty
sources.source: Treaty concerning the Archipelago of Spitsbergen, 1920, Article 1 and signatories: USA, the British Empire (with Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India also signing), Denmark, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden

sources.claim: Article 9 bans any naval base or fortification
sources.source: Spitsbergen Treaty, 1920, Article 9

sources.claim: Taxes raised on Svalbard may only be spent on Svalbard
sources.source: Spitsbergen Treaty, 1920, Article 8

sources.claim: Norway's own Svalbard tax rules keep rates low
sources.source: Norwegian Tax Administration, Svalbard tax rules (Svalbardskatteloven, 1996)

sources.claim: Soviet Russia was absent from Paris; Moscow recognised Norway's sovereignty in 1924
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbardtraktaten'; Soviet note of 16 February 1924

sources.claim: Norway formally took over on 14 August 1925
sources.source: Svalbard Act (Svalbardloven), 17 July 1925, in force 14 August 1925

sources.claim: Arktikugol bought the Barentsburg mine from its Dutch owners in 1932
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Barentsburg'

sources.claim: Settlements were evacuated in 1941 and attacked by German warships in 1943
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbard under andre verdenskrig'

sources.claim: After 1945 Norwegian and Soviet miners returned and the settlements were rebuilt
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbard under andre verdenskrig', 'Longyearbyen' and 'Barentsburg'

sources.claim: In November 1944 Molotov asked Norway for joint defence and for Bear Island
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbardsaken 1944-1947'; Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs archives

sources.claim: Norway's parliament declined in February 1947; the 1920 treaty area stayed unchanged
sources.source: Storting resolution, February 1947; Store norske leksikon, 'Svalbardsaken 1944-1947'

sources.claim: Bear Island lies about 420 km from the North Cape
sources.source: Great-circle distance Bjørnøya (74.43°N, 19.03°E) to Nordkapp (71.17°N, 25.78°E)

sources.claim: Bear Island and the gap to mainland Norway lie beside the route of Russia's Northern Fleet from its Kola Peninsula bases to the Atlantic
sources.source: Norwegian Intelligence Service, 'Focus 2024' annual threat assessment (Northern Fleet, Barents Sea and the Bear Island gap); Northern Fleet headquarters at Severomorsk

sources.claim: In 1977 Norway set a 200-nautical-mile fisheries protection zone around Svalbard
sources.source: Royal Decree of 3 June 1977 on the fisheries protection zone around Svalbard

sources.claim: The zone covers about 804,000 km², some thirteen times the land
sources.source: Norwegian Directorate of Fisheries: Svalbard fisheries protection zone about 804,000 km²

sources.claim: Norway lets other fleets fish under Norwegian quotas and inspections
sources.source: Norwegian White Paper Meld. St. 32 (2015-2016); Norwegian Coast Guard

sources.claim: Norway's territorial waters around Svalbard are 12 nautical miles (since 2004)
sources.source: Royal Decree on Svalbard territorial waters, in force 1 January 2004

sources.claim: Norway says the zone and seabed fall under the UN Law of the Sea, not the treaty's equal rights
sources.source: Norwegian White Paper Meld. St. 32 (2015-2016) Svalbard

sources.claim: The UN Law of the Sea is the 1982 ocean treaty
sources.source: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Montego Bay, 10 December 1982

sources.claim: Russia does not recognise the zone; Iceland, Spain and the EU have challenged how Norway applies it
sources.source: Pedersen, T., 'The Svalbard Continental Shelf Controversy', Ocean Development & International Law, 2009; Meld. St. 32 (2015-2016)

sources.claim: In February 2019 the Supreme Court ruled a Latvian vessel needed a Norwegian licence for snow crab
sources.source: Supreme Court of Norway, HR-2019-282-S, 14 February 2019

sources.claim: More than 100 antennas at SvalSat, one of the world's largest satellite ground stations, contacting polar-orbiting satellites on every pass
sources.source: Kongsberg Satellite Services (KSAT), SvalSat station information

sources.claim: Two subsea fibre cables completed in 2004
sources.source: Space Norway, Svalbard Undersea Cable System

sources.claim: In January 2022 one of the two cables was damaged; no cause publicly named
sources.source: Space Norway statement, January 2022; Norwegian Police, Troms district, 2022

sources.claim: In 2017 Russia's foreign ministry protested a NATO parliamentary meeting held in Longyearbyen
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement, October 2017, on the NATO Parliamentary Assembly committee meeting in Longyearbyen; reported by High North News, October 2017

sources.claim: In February 2020, at the treaty's centenary, Lavrov wrote to Norway
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, letter of February 2020; reported by Reuters, February 2020

sources.claim: Russia's foreign ministry says Norway's rules and restrictions on Russian activity breach the treaty's equal treatment
sources.source: Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Lavrov letter to Norway's foreign minister and accompanying statements, February 2020; reported by Reuters and The Barents Observer, February 2020

sources.claim: Norway replied no bilateral talks were needed and its rules apply equally
sources.source: Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs reply, February 2020; reported by High North News

sources.claim: Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 and stores more than 1.2 million samples
sources.source: Crop Trust and Norwegian Ministry of Agriculture and Food, Svalbard Global Seed Vault figures, 2024

sources.claim: Svalbard's yearly average temperature rose 3 to 5 °C between 1971 and 2017
sources.source: Norwegian Centre for Climate Services, 'Climate in Svalbard 2100', 2019

sources.claim: Sea ice around Svalbard has shrunk
sources.source: Norwegian Polar Institute, Environmental Monitoring of Svalbard and Jan Mayen (MOSJ)

sources.claim: Longyearbyen shut its coal power plant in October 2023
sources.source: Longyearbyen Community Council, October 2023

sources.claim: Fish stocks such as cod and mackerel are shifting north
sources.source: Norwegian Institute of Marine Research, Barents Sea ecosystem reports

sources.claim: Norway has not opened the seabed around Svalbard to oil and gas
sources.source: Norwegian Offshore Directorate, licensing maps

sources.claim: The treaty was written before any aircraft had flown over the North Pole (first: airship Norge, May 1926)
sources.source: Store norske leksikon, 'Norge (luftskip)'

sources.claim: 'High North, low tension'; Russia's 'Arctic: Territory of Dialogue'
sources.source: Norwegian government High North strategy; Russian international Arctic forum 'The Arctic: Territory of Dialogue'
